summary: In Greek mythology and Athenian topography, Ilissus (Ilisos) is the river of Athens that once flowed outside the walls toward Phaleron, and a river-god associated with its banks. Myth links the stream to Boreas' abduction of Orithyia and to the sacred landscape of Agrai and Cynosarges; Plato's Phaedrus sets Socrates' talk under plane trees by its waters. Distinct from the Kephisos, Athens' other great stream.
etymology: Greek Ιλισός / Ilisós; the -sós/-ttós ending is widely taken as Pre-Greek substratum, shared with other Attic toponyms.
cultCenters: Ardittos / Cynosarges (sanctuary of the river as demi-god)
Banks by the Olympieion and Kallirhoe spring

sections.heading: River and river-god
paragraphs: The Ilissus drains the western slopes of Hymettus and in antiquity ran outside Athens' walls — Plato's Critias names it among the borders of the early circuit. Its grassy, plane-shaded banks were remembered as idyllic teaching ground for Socrates. Local tradition treated Ilissus as a demi-god, son of Poseidon and Demeter, worshipped on Ardittos near the Panathenaic Stadium.

Hyginus lists him among the Rivers born to Oceanus and Tethys; Apollodorus and Apollonius place Orithyia's abduction by Boreas beside this stream — the birth setting of the Boread twins Zetes and Calais.

sections.heading: Sacred banks
paragraphs: The Ilissus corridor held shrines of Artemis Agrotera at Agrai (linked to Marathon rites and the Lesser Mysteries), Pan, and other Attic cults; the spring Kallirhoe lay nearby. Modern Athens covered most of the bed as a storm drain, though stretches near the Olympieion remain visible and restoration plans have been discussed.
The atlas id ilissus is the mythic Potamos and Athenian sacred river — not a modern hydrology article alone.
